summary: Defines a new BGP extended community type that carries a 4-octet AS number.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines a BGP extended community that can include a four-octet Autonomous System number. It also assigns type values for route targets and route origins and recommends that two-octet ASes keep using the older format.

questions: what is a 4-octet as extended community
what is bgp route target type 0x0202
what is a four-octet as-specific community
how is the four-octet community formatted
subtitle: A BGP extended community format that carries a four-octet Autonomous System number.

tldr.problem: The existing two-octet AS-specific community format cannot carry a four-octet Autonomous System number.
tldr.mechanism: The new format puts a four-octet AS number in the Global Administrator field and reserves two octets for a subtype-defined Local Administrator value.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines transitive and non-transitive types and assigns values for route target and route origin communities.

today: RFC 5668 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Four-Octet Community Is Needed
sections.content: A BGP extended community carries information associated with routes. This RFC defines a four-octet AS-specific extended community, similar to the two-octet form but able to carry a four-octet Autonomous System (AS) number.
sections.plainLanguage: The new community keeps the same general purpose as the older AS-specific form. It has room for a four-octet AS number.

sections.title: Fields in the Extended Community
sections.content:
The extended type has a two-octet Type field and a six-octet Value field. The high-order type octet is 0x02 for transitive communities or 0x42 for non-transitive communities; the low-order octet identifies the subtype.

The Value field contains a four-octet Global Administrator field with an IANA-assigned AS number and a two-octet Local Administrator field. The organization identified by the AS number can encode information in the local field, whose format and meaning should be defined by the subtype.
sections.plainLanguage: The type identifies whether the community is transitive and which subtype it uses. The value carries the AS number and a smaller field whose meaning comes from that subtype.

sections.title: Compatibility With Two-Octet AS Numbers
sections.content:
A two-octet AS number can be represented in the four-octet field by setting its two high-order octets to zero. But a two-octet and four-octet community with the same subtype and Local Administrator value would still be treated as different communities.

To preserve backward compatibility and avoid inconsistencies, ASes using two-octet AS numbers SHOULD use the two-octet AS-specific communities instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A two-octet AS could fit in the new format, but the two community forms would not be treated as identical. The RFC recommends that two-octet ASes continue using the two-octet form.

sections.title: Registered Types and Security
sections.content:
The RFC establishes an IANA registry for four-octet AS-specific extended communities. It assigns 0x0202 to the four-octet AS-specific Route Target and 0x0203 to the four-octet AS-specific Route Origin. The registry also defines ranges for transitive and non-transitive type values.

The RFC adds no new security issues beyond those for BGP extended communities. It notes a potential serious issue involving malformed optional transitive attributes and refers to separate guidance on that issue.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA records the subtype values defined here. The memo says the usual BGP extended-community security considerations still apply.

references.text: Sangli, S., Tappan, D., and Y. Rekhter, "BGP Extended Communities Attribute", RFC 4360, February 2006.
